note: Thirty-six things this archive published and had to take back, with what caused each. They are gathered here because the pattern in the right-hand column is the most useful thing on the site: a family history that only shows its conclusions is asking to be believed on trust.

causes.population: A negative built from a list mistaken for a population — the archive searched what it happened to have and reported the answer as though it had searched everything.
causes.scope: A search run over part of the ground and written up as though it covered all of it.
causes.circular: A fact derived from a reference, written into the record, and then cited back as evidence.
causes.tree: A claim taken from the family tree and repeated before it was tested.
causes.reading: A document read wrongly, or a conclusion drawn past what the document says.
causes.process: A mistake in the archive's own working — a bug, a bad build, or a word used loosely.

rows: Three Booyzens listed together as deaths in concentration camps

ONLY TWO OF THE THREE DIED IN A CAMP. Read on the University of Cape Town database's own pages rather than through two intermediaries: Gert Jacobus (Johannesburg RC, aged 2, farm Rietvallei, district Marico) and Gertruida Magdalena (Vereeniging RC, aged 19, farm Rietvlei, district Heidelberg) are each recorded “died in camp: YES”. JAN GERHARDUS LODEWICUS, AGED 2, IS RECORDED “DIED IN CAMP: NO”, with no camp and no farm attached at all. Listing the three together was this archive's compression, not the database's — and it is the same failure as reading an index line as though it were the record. Gertruida's entry also carries the note “or Irene RC”, so even her camp is uncertain.
The National Archives' catalogue given as “national.archives.gov.za/naairs.htm”

THE LIVE DOMAIN HAS NO DOT IN IT — nationalarchives.gov.za. The host as published has no address record and no mail record at all. It appeared in the note of 13 September that ends “written down because the wrong address cost this archive a day”, which is the row that exists to stop exactly this. Found by a tool written to check whether the sources this site cites are still there; it looks for hosts named in PROSE as well as in links, because this archive writes its sources in sentences.
“WILLEM HERMANUS PIETERZEN — Anna Catharina Slier's FIRST husband”

HE IS THE SON. De Villiers's volume 3 gives “HERMANUS PIETERSEN, namen van ouders onbekend, gehuwd 5 April 1807 met ANNA CATHARINA SLIER”, and their children as “1 Willem Hermanus, gedoopt 12 Maart 1809; 2 Johan Christiaan, gedoopt 28 April 1810”. THIS ARCHIVE BUILT ONE MAN OUT OF TWO DOCUMENTS THAT SPELL HIM DIFFERENTLY — the 1817 marriage register's HARMANUS PIETERZE and the 1840 death notice's WILLIAM PIETERSEN — and a long name looked like a way to reconcile them. The husband is Hermanus; Willem Hermanus is the boy baptised in 1809. This archive half knew, because its own note already called the 1851 godfather “his son”. THE NAMING CLAIM SURVIVES AND IMPROVES: Willem Hermanus is Willem for his mother's father, Willem Slier of Hamburg, and Hermanus for his own father. A SECOND HALF-BROTHER, JOHAN CHRISTIAAN, WAS INVISIBLE FOR AS LONG AS THE TWO MEN WERE ONE.
“LUUS with BOOYZEN returns NOTHING” — published against the five unplaced Silverton children

IT RETURNS A MARRIAGE. The Marriage Transcription Database on gendatabase.com: “1928 · CORNELIUS ABRAHAM LUUS × SUSANNA FREDERIK ALETTHA BOOYZEN”. The negative was TRUE OF NAAIRS, which is the only index this archive had asked, and it was published as though it were true of the record. A MARRIAGE REGISTER IS NOT AN ESTATE INDEX. A sentence that says “returns nothing” has to name what was asked, and this one did not. Whether this Susanna is the “Ousie” of the Silverton pillar is a separate question and is not being assumed.
Leeuwberg pinned at FAURESMITH, on a 1903 land file naming a “LEEUWBERG NO 465, DIST. FAURISMITH”

IT IS A DIFFERENT FARM OF THE SAME NAME. The Friend of the Free State of 13 January 1870 advertises “the farm, WILDEBEESTKOOI, ADJOINING THE FARM LEEUBERG, THE PROPERTY OF THE LATE J.G.E. KOLBE, ABOUT TWO HOURS RIDE FROM THE TOWN OF BLOEMFONTEIN”. Fifteen or twenty kilometres, not a hundred and thirty. The pin stood for two days, and it was published with its own objection printed beside it — that Fauresmith is 130 km from Kaalspruit while the obituary says he died at one and lies at the other. THE OBJECTION WAS THE RIGHT ONE AND IT HAS ANSWERED AGAINST THE PIN. Moved to Bloemfontein, still approximate. The two-farm contradiction this archive could not reconcile was never a contradiction: Leeuberg and Kaalspruit are neighbours.
“1898 — JGL Booyzen of Kwaggafontein, district Marico, IN THE FIELD-CORNET'S PAPERS”

THE PAPERS ARE THE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT'S. The atlas has carried that line under Marico since the entry was built. The three documents behind it are TAB source OD — the school files of the South African Republic — and they are a subsidy application, book orders and quarterly returns for a farm school. A field-cornet does appear in the bundle, exactly once, valuing the teacher's dwelling in May 1898, and that is a different document sent by a different man. The line was written from a memory of the record rather than from the record. CORRECTED IN PLACE, and the record is now eight documents instead of three.
Margaret Downing “c. 1804, London” — and, for a day, a death date thrown into doubt by a newspaper

THE STONE HAD BOTH ANSWERS AND THIS ARCHIVE HAD THE STONE. The Burgersdorp monument has been on the Kolbe page for weeks, photographed and captioned; the caption quoted it as far as “ALSO HIS RELICT MARGARET DOWNING…” AND STOPPED. The next two lines read “BORN IN LONDON 23 FEBRUARY 1803 AND DIED AT BURGHERSDORP 2_ NOVEMBER 1867.” Her birth moves from a guessed year to a date. AND THE DEATH WAS NEVER IN DOUBT: yesterday's Grahamstown Journal obituary said she died “about three months since” — January 1868 — and this archive published the discrepancy rather than resolving it. It was nearly five months, and a journalist rounding is a journalist rounding. THE FAULT IS THE CAPTION: a transcription that stops before the end of an inscription is not a transcription, and this one hid two facts in plain sight for weeks.
“148 rows read of 184 — THIRTY-SIX DOCUMENTS WERE NOT REACHED, and this archive is not going to call 148 a complete enumeration”

The caution was right in spirit and wrong in fact, and the fact is worse. ALL TEN PAGES HAD BEEN WALKED. The thirty-six were not unreached — THEY WERE THROWN AWAY BY THIS ARCHIVE'S OWN ROW FILTER, which required a description field longer than three characters and so silently dropped every row whose description column the index leaves short or blank. Re-run without that condition the same query returns 194 rows, 184 of them unique: THE EXACT COUNT. This archive published a scope caveat that blamed the source for a hole it had dug itself — which is the same failure as the blank Name column, one layer up: A FILTER THAT DROPS WHAT IT DOES NOT RECOGNISE LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE AN ARCHIVE THAT DOES NOT HOLD IT. The thirty-six turn out to include SEVEN ANGLO-BOER WAR COMPENSATION CLAIMS BY BOOYZENS IN THE MARICO DISTRICT.
Martha Angeline Kolbe, sixty days old, was “BURIED AT VOLKSRUST”, and Volksrust held a concentration camp

Both halves withdrawn, six hours after publishing. HER STONE IS IN WAKKERSTROOM MAIN CEMETERY. The index this archive read gives the burial as “Volksrust, Eastvaal District Council, Mpumalanga” — and that is a DISTRICT MUNICIPALITY, not a town; Wakkerstroom lies inside it. This archive read a modern administrative area as a place of burial, which is a failure of reading and not of the source. WITH THE TOWN GOES THE CAMP. The stone reads “TER GEDACHTENIS VAN ONS GELIEFDE KLEINE”, in Dutch, and the mason's town is cut across its base: NEWCASTLE, twenty-five miles away in Natal. A family stone in a town churchyard, cut by a monumental mason in another colony, is not a camp burial. The care taken in the original entry — “records the burial place without claiming the camp” — was not enough, because naming the camp at all in an entry about a child who died in December 1901 makes the claim whatever the sentence says.
The 1902 prisoner of war could not be assigned to either George Augustus Kolbe of Wakkerstroom

Now it can, and the withdrawal of the morning is replaced by an answer rather than a shrug. BOTH MEN ARE BURIED IN THE SAME CEMETERY and both stones are read. The younger: “GEORGE AUGUSTUS — GEB. 29 JULIE 1863 — OORL. 28 SEPT. 1954”, which is the Colesberg font date to the day. The elder: “GEORGE AUGUSTUS KOLBE — GEB. 2 OKTOBER 1861 — OORL. 8 NOVEMBER 1934”. THE POW RECORD SAYS AGE 40, EVENT 1902. A man born 2 October 1861 was forty from October 1901 to October 1902; a man born 29 July 1863 was thirty-nine for the whole of 1902. THE PRISONER IS THE ELDER MAN. This is recorded as a correction rather than quietly fixed, because the archive published a claim, withdrew it, and then reversed the withdrawal, all in one day, and a reader is owed the whole of that.
George Augustus Kolbe of Wakkerstroom, born Colesberg 1863, was a prisoner of war in 1902 — “the fourth man of this family taken in that war”

Withdrawn within the hour, and by the same record that produced it. The POW entry — WO 108/368, the master list of Boer prisoners numbers 1 to 32561 — gives RESIDENCE WAKKERSTROOM, which is what the claim was built on, and this archive stopped reading there. It also gives AGE 40, NATIONALITY TRANSVAALER, PRISON NATAL. The man baptised at Colesberg on 11 October 1863 was THIRTY-NINE in 1902. A SECOND GEORGE AUGUSTUS KOLBE, born at Burgersdorp in 1861 and dead at Standerton in 1934, was forty or forty-one that year — and his own marriage entry to Susanna Margaretha Swart gives his residence as Wakkerstroom too. Two men of one name in one town, which this archive had itself written down as a warning in the same hour, in the same run of searches, and then walked straight past. THE PRISONER IS MORE PROBABLY THE OLDER MAN. Nothing decides it but the age, and an index age is a weak thing; so the claim is withdrawn rather than reassigned.
The Wonderboom deeds register showed a transfer from M. J. Booyzen, widow, to David Schalk Booyzen on 9 April 1907

The transferor is right and the date is not. Her gravestone at Rebecca Street, Pretoria, reads “MAGDALENA JOHANNA BOOYZEN (GEB. BEZUIDENHOUT), GEB. 8 MEI 1870, OORL. 29 JAN 1955” — so the ledger's “8/5/1870” beside her name is HER BIRTH DATE, which identifies her beyond doubt. But her husband PETRUS JACOBUS BOOYZEN died on 25 MARCH 1947, so she was not a widow in 1907 and cannot have transferred anything as one that year. The 9 April 1907 read off that row belongs to a different row: the ledger's columns were mis-aligned in the reading. What survives is the identification; what is withdrawn is the date, and with it the suggestion that David Schalk Booysen could be carried to 1907.
Both testable POW ages run one to two years high against this archive's dates

That described the De List, not the record. The fuller register gives Stefanus Francois as 26 — exact against a birth of about October 1874 — and David Schalk as 53, within weeks of his fifty-third birthday on 9 June 1848. The De List's 28 and 54 are the outliers. The caveat was published on the strength of the weaker of two documents before the stronger had been found.
The De List's prisoner numbers are a separate series and do not locate these men in the fuller register

They are the same series and they locate them exactly. The claim came from misreading a leading digit: image 139 of item 1 begins at 19431, not 18431, which the batch title on image 136 states outright — “Nos. 19,431 to 20,705”. The de Beer entries read as 18463–18465 were 19463–19465. In the correct batch, image 126, numbers 18463, 18464 and 18465 are STEFANUS FRANCOIS, PETRUS JACOBUS and DAVID SCHALK BOOYSEN.
Catherine Maria Sophia is a Barry name

It is a KOLBE name. The 1848 Graaff-Reinet baptism register, entry 603, names the godmother in full as CATHARINE SOPHIA MARIA KOLBER — eleven years before her sister named the daughter this archive had been treating as the head of the chain. The namesakes page called it “a Barry name that outlives the Barry surname by eighty years”; it outlives the Kolbe surname instead, and the archive already held the woman, filed as plain “Catharine Kolbe”, without noticing she carried the name first.
A relationship search had found one name the Barry notices never gave

It found none. HENRY JAONAS BARRY is JAMES HENRY BARRY, who was already in this archive — the same baptism indexed twice, once as Henry Jaonas with the year read as 1868 and once as HENNERY JAMES BERRY with it read as 1848. Same birth date, same parents, and FamilySearch attaches both to one tree person. The register itself decides: “Graaff-Reinet. Baptism Records 1846–1851” cannot hold an 1868 entry. So the “baptised at twenty years old” that made him interesting was a mis-transcribed year, and “Jaonas” was a mis-read “James” — which is what the archive's own register search implied when it found JONAS nowhere among the Barrys or Kolbes. The eleven-against-nine gap is unchanged: TWO children are still missing, not one.
Magdelena Elisabeth de Beer was carried here under WikiTree's codes, b6c2 and b6c6

The codes are b5c2 and b5c6. de Villiers 1893 page 34 puts ZACCHARIAS DE BEER — her father — as the FIFTH child of Matthijs Andries de Beer, not the sixth, and Pieter van Zyl said so on G2G before the book was opened; reading page 34 confirmed it. The b6 is WikiTree's, and this archive repeated it for a day without checking it in print. It matters more than a digit: a de Villiers code is an address, and quoting the wrong one sends the next reader to the wrong family. Where this archive QUOTES the WikiTree profile it still says b6, because that is what the profile says — the error being reported is not the same as the error being made.
The two Magdalena de Beers were two different women, and the tree had merged them

They are one woman. de Villiers 1893, page 34, marks ONLY the second — Magdalena baptised 16 October 1754 — with “zie Booijsen”, and 1754 is the birth year this archive has always carried for its own Magdelena Elisabeth. The argument published here for a day ran the other way: that Jan Booysen's wife was dead by December 1793 while ours died in 1843, so they could not be the same. The 1843 death date is the weak link, not the identity — this archive's own page said both her dates came off the family tree with no source stated. What actually followed from reading the book is the opposite of what was published: she married JAN, and generation seven is now in question rather than confirmed.
A relationship search had turned up two Barry children on neither parent's death notice

It turned up one. WILLIAM FREDERICK THOMAS BARRY, baptised 29 September 1861, was already recorded on William Barry's own page — put there the day the Burgersdorp doopregister was read, with the doubt stated in the same sentence. The search re-surfaced him and this archive wrote him up as a find for about an hour. Only HENRY JAONAS BARRY is new. The section now says which is which, and the header no longer counts him.
Hendrik Stephanus Nicolaas Booyen was buried at Johannesburg

He was buried at ROODEPOORT–MARAISBURG, twenty kilometres west, in the Central Cemetery there — section I D.R., entry 96. The FamilySearch collection is titled “Johannesburg Cemetery Records” and the index repeats that label for every register inside it, including those of other municipalities. The collection title is not the place.
Anna J. Mary Booyzen and George Downing Daschner were stillborn or died the same day

Both lived. She was SIX MONTHS old and he was THREE MONTHS AND FIVE DAYS. The Brixton register keeps Years, Months and Days in three separate columns and FamilySearch's index collapses them into one field, so a child with the Years column blank comes out as “0 days”. This archive printed the index reading for an afternoon without opening the page.
Only a family tree puts Anna Maria van der Merwe in this family

A Dutch Reformed baptism does. Her son DAVID SCHALK BOOIJZEN was born 12 December 1806 and christened on 4 January 1807, with PIETER JACOBUS BOOIJZEN and ANNA MARIA VAN DER MERWE named as his parents — and he is first of the eight on the 1876 Sterfkennis. The wall on the ancestor chart said the wrong thing for a day and has been rewritten.
No Booyzen filed a war-losses compensation claim

One did. This archive searched the War Losses Compensation Commission, found nothing, and published the zero while noting it was weak because the Commission's records are catalogued by sub-commissioner and not by claimant. David Schalk Booijzen's answer to question ten of his wife's 1900 death notice is “none. Compensation claim filed.” The claim exists; it was the finding aid that could not reach it.
Anna Catharina Johanna Olivier was on this site twice

One woman, two records: a stub written from the 1908 death notice — “His first wife, named as pre-deceased” — and a full record written from her own 1891 Sterfkennis hours later. The shared-name page gathered them as though they were two people. Merged. The build now warns on every shared name so a human checks each one reads as two lives and not one.

She died on 6 February 1902, at Driefontein in Groot Marico, and her own Death Notice 844 says so. It also gives her father as Jacob Dormehl, her mother as unknown, her age as 60 years 4 months, her estate as one wagon and her furniture, and THREE husbands where this archive had one — Jacob van Staden, Matthys Roos, then Booysen.
Anna Johanna Booijzen, born Alberts, died at Boekfontein and is not this family

Every clause of that was wrong. She is Anna Catharina Johanna OLIVIER, she died at BRAKFONTEIN — the family's own farm, where the archive's oldest document was written — and she is the first wife of Hendrik Stefanus Booijsen. The maiden name reads Oliefier and contains no b, r, t or s; her son gives OLIVIER on the 1908 notice. Two misreadings on one page kept a documented wife, seven children and a whole Olivier line off this site for a week.
Hendrik Stefanus Booysen had four children

He had at least seven. His first wife's 1891 Sterfkennis lists them all, of age: Petrus Jacobus, Ocken Johannes, Anna Johanna Maria, Elesabettha Maria Cornelya, Alettha Catrina Johanna, Magdalena Johanna and Hendrick Stefanus Nicolaas. The 1908 notice names four because by 1908 only four were left.
Hendrik Stefanus Booysen's four children were his second wife's

They were his first wife's. The Zeerust marriage register, entry 13, dates the second marriage to 14 April 1892 and gives the bride's age as fifty-one and her condition as widow. By 1908 all four children were adults, two of them married women. The archive put them under the marriage it could name rather than the marriage that could have produced them.
Margarietha Wilhelmina Elizabeth Barry was John Augustus Barry I’s daughter

She was his granddaughter. The 1915 death notice names eight children and she is not among them; her father is Hendrik Nicholaas Barry, whose other children were baptised at Dordrecht and Slang River between 1888 and 1900. Moved down a generation — which is where the cousin marriage of 1924 needs her to be, and the archive had her in the wrong place while asserting it.
The 1915 notice named eight children and the archive listed nine

Two men on that list — John Augustus Barry II and George Augustus Barry — had no page at all, while a ninth name stood in their place. All three fixed together; the build now refuses to publish a household naming somebody who does not exist.
The ancestor chart, every wife one generation too high

The chart put each man's wife in his mother's box. Kathleen Barry stood as Willem Hermanus Booyzen's mother when she was his wife; Johanna Catharina Mountjoy stood as Petrus Jacobus Booysen's mother when she was his; and the woman at the root had no mother drawn at all. Four slots, all shifted by one. Rebuilt, and the genuinely empty slot — the mother of the 1812 man — is now a wall.
One did. The 1915 death notice lists the siblings and there is no second.
No document anywhere names a family farm. The name came off the tree and had nothing behind it.
Eighteen. Her father died in December 1947 and she was born in March 1929.
1906. A baptism register and her own death form agree against the tree, and the tree had mistranscribed one digit.
The Farm List returns nothing, so the farm was not burned
The negative was VOID. The register searched turns out to be an Orange Free State land roll that does not cover the Cape at all.
The tree contradicts itself on 1827 and 1840
It does not. 1827 is when James Montjoy died and 1840 is when the notice was filed. The contradiction was the archive's.
The z was this family's invention
The 1851 Graaff-Reinet register writes a neighbouring family's name with a z in the same hand and ink. The z was Cape Dutch orthography before it was anybody's statement.
Willem Hermanus is a Booyzen name
It is a Pieterzen name. It came in through a step-relation with no blood tie to this family at all, and four generations have carried it.
A distribution chart with nine provinces
Five of the nine had been filled in by the archive itself. The source reports four. The chart now draws four, and a dash where nothing was reported.
It did not. Auto-linking injected HTML anchors into an SVG and silently erased half the names in it. It did not look broken; it looked plausible.

All twenty-two dated 1930 or later were read. The twenty before 1930 were not, and they held James Mountjoy's wills of 1818 and 1827 and an 1834 Colonial Office memorial. A filter applied for convenience was written up as the whole search.
It was sent, and one of the two addresses bounced at the server. Sent and delivered are not the same word and this archive used the wrong one.
The 1905 clerk's Booysen proves the family used an s
It proves nothing. Seven Attorney-General files spell one Middelburg constable both ways, twice inside 1905. Only the son's signature still carries weight.
They hold 184. Every search in the project had been run against the Cape depot alone, one repository out of nine, for weeks.
14 October. Her father wrote it on her mother's death notice three months before he was widowed.
1944 is the one time the form worked
The very next document opened named both parents too. The claim was a count of documents read, dressed as a count of documents that exist.
The Marico Booyzens are not this family
The direct ancestor died in district Rustenburg in 1876, twenty-five years before the war. The reason for holding the two clusters apart has gone; the atlas now says unresolved.

There is one. A son was a MIJNWERKER of Dugmore Mijn at Indwe in 1908. The negative was built out of six occupations the archive happened to have read, and it had not read his because it did not know the man existed.
He died in the Transvaal at about thirty
Estate O/2899 belongs to his uncle, born 1818. The death date had no source but the file number: the archive read a year off a reference, wrote it in as a fact, and cited the fact back.

31 March 1930. 1943 is the year her husband finally filed — thirteen years late. The same mistake as O/2899, made in the same way, and found the same afternoon by opening the document instead of trusting the reference.
John Augustus Barry was born at sea

Born in IRELAND. The 1903 registration of his death, made by the son who was present, enters him as “Irishman born in Ireland”. The 1915 notice this archive had been using was sworn by another son twelve years later and says “at sea, exact whereabouts unknown”. The archive had the weaker document and had not looked for a better one.

25 August 1903, as the family tree said all along. The 1915 notice gives the 3rd; the statutory registration, signed by a son present at the death, gives the 25th. For once the tree was right and the document this archive preferred was wrong.
Dorothea Regina Barry was a daughter of John Barry

She is not on the 1915 death notice. This archive said she was “named on” it, having quoted four lines from the top of the page without reading the children's list at the bottom. The only Dorothea Regina in the registers is a granddaughter, baptised at Slang River in 1892.
Ruben Jacobus Josuah Barry was a son of John Barry
Also not on the notice. A Ruben Jacobus Hosea was baptised at Dordrecht in 1888 — a grandson. The Schoeman name Ruben does come into this family, one generation later than this archive said.
Johan Gottlieb Kolbe was buried at the German church of the Savoy, entry 55, grave 7

Taken from a family tree and repeated here. The Westminster Burials register, held by the City of Westminster Archives Centre, has him DIED 18 NOVEMBER 1845 AND BURIED 26 NOVEMBER 1845 AT ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, GREAT MARLBOROUGH STREET, page 7. The date matches to the day and the seven matches; the church does not. The register also gives a death date and a birth year of 1764, neither of which this archive had.
Johan Gottlieb Kolbe had one wife, called Mary

He had two, and both were called Mary — which is why one of them could never be made to fit a run of baptisms from 1792 to 1819. The first died 2 August 1814 aged 46; the second died 15 August 1824 aged 36. Both are in the German Lutheran Church register, TNA RG 4/4631.
R_177176049779 is this archive's reference for Petrus Jacobus Booysen's 1812 birth

It was recorded once, from a FindMyPast search run without a subscription, and never opened. Opened twice on a live full subscription, FindMyPast's own transcript page returns a 500 error. THE REFERENCE DOES NOT RESOLVE. It stays on the page as a struck citation rather than being quietly deleted.
The German Savoy registers are RG 4/4625, 4626, 4628 and 4631 for burials

RG 4/4630 belongs on that list too. The 1807 burial of Charles Samuel Kolbe is entered in both 4631 and 4630, with the same death date and the same age to the day — a register and its duplicate. The archive's own note named five volumes and missed one.
Seventeen people had a page saying they are “not yet discussed on any page”

Among them GEORGE AUGUSTUS KOLBE, the 1820 Settler, named 155 times in the built site; JOHN BARRY, 158; GEORGE MOUNTJOY, 140; PETRUS JACOBUS BOOYSEN, 110; JOHANNA CATHARINA MOUNTJOY, 89. THE DATA WAS FINE AND THE BUILD THREW IT AWAY. dossiers.py dropped any name that was a strict prefix of a longer person’s name — a rule written to stop “John Barry” swallowing “John Barry Booyzen”, which instead silenced the shorter man entirely. The fix keeps the shorter name and fences it with a negative lookahead, so it matches everywhere except where the longer name begins. 2,428 mentions came back. NOTHING REFUSED THE BUILD WHILE THIS WAS TRUE, so a gate now does: checkregisters.py fails when a person the dossier calls undiscussed is named in the built pages. Found because the estate asked this archive to look for a fault the Mazza archive had just had.
WO 12/1430 is the muster book to read for James Mountjoy

It is the 20TH AND 21ST DRAGOONS FOR 1867–1868 — fifty years after he was discharged, and the re-raised regiment rather than the one that garrisoned the Cape. The 21st Light Dragoons has a continuous WO 12 run of its own and the piece that covers his discharge is WO 12/1450, 1816–1817. THE WRONG REFERENCE HAD BEEN WRITTEN INTO A LETTER TO KEW; the letter was still unsent and now names the right piece and says an earlier version had it wrong.
The 21st Light Dragoons left the Cape in 1816

September 1817. An extract of a letter from the Cape dated 1 and 10 September 1817, printed in the Sun, the Star, the Public Ledger, the Morning Herald and the Hampshire Chronicle that November: “the 21st Light Dragoons have embarked for India”. The 1816 figure was written on 15 September with no source attached and stood in three files. IT MATTERS BECAUSE HE MARRIED IN MARCH 1817 — under 1816 he was already a civilian when he married, and under 1817 he had six months to choose between a wife at Graaff-Reinet and a transport to Madras.
The Burgersdorp sweep of images 605–818 found five new people

Three. Johanna Catharina Mountjoy, born 28 January 1860, was already held in full — a daughter of George Mountjoy who married William Henry Keys — and the sweep only confirmed her and gave her a reference. Frederick Fortunatus Werdmuller was already held from a 1907 petition and a 1953 estate; what the sweep added was his birth and his mother, which is a real gain and not a new person. THE DUPLICATE PERSON RECORDS WERE CAUGHT BY THE BUILD'S OWN NAME-COLLISION CHECK for the first and by reading the register for the second, before either reached a page. The rule it costs: a sweep that returns a name is checked against the archive before it is called a find.
MSB 751 is a letter written to George Augustus Kolbe “on his ordination”

It is not. The National Library’s catalogue described it that way and this archive repeated the catalogue without ever asking whether the date fitted. The DSAB draft that came with the letter dates the ordination to 25 MAY 1833 — two years and nine months after the letter of 23 August 1830 — and the letter itself says George had been “fully accepted by the [L.M.S.] as one of their Missionaries”, which is a different step. THERE WERE THREE STEPS AND THE ARCHIVE HAD COLLAPSED THEM INTO ONE: mission assistant on 8 February 1828, accepted as a missionary in the summer of 1830, ordained by Arbousset and Casalis on 25 May 1833. A CATALOGUE DESCRIPTION IS A FINDING AID, NOT THE DOCUMENT. This archive quoted one as though it were the second, and the document itself corrected it the day it arrived.
The Settler’s parentage — father AND mother — is on the parish register

The father is. The mother is not. The Westminster baptism of 2 February 1803 names “John Gottlob and Mary”, and “Mary” is all it gives, at that font and at eight others in the same family. The German Lutheran burial register of 1814 gives her death, her burial and her age of 46 and NO MAIDEN NAME. “MARY LARMAN” COMES FROM THE FAMILY TREE AND FROM NOWHERE ELSE THIS ARCHIVE HAS READ — and this archive’s own person record has said so all along (“her surname before marriage is not known and no marriage has been found”), while the page beside it put the tree’s surname inside a sentence ending “is on the parish register” and chipped it Documented. THE DATA WAS RIGHT AND THE PROSE WAS WRONG. Found while testing a FamilySearch memory of 2017 that makes the same claim; the search engine returned this archive’s own repository as the authority for it, WHICH IS WHAT CIRCULARITY LOOKS LIKE FROM THE INSIDE.
The DSAB typescript is unsigned, and this archive will not name its author

IT IS UNSIGNED. THE EMAIL THAT CARRIED IT IS NOT. Melanie Geustyn of the National Library, with the Background File open in front of her, wrote: “I am also sharing with you a two page document that was written for the DSAB … The author, KS, WOULD BE DR. KAREL SCHOEMAN who worked here at the National Library.” This archive opened the two attachments, read four pages of manuscript and two of typescript, reasoned its way to Schoeman from the inside — the Bethanie claim has only his 1985 book behind it, and the paper was typed where he worked — and published the attribution as an inference it would not assert. THE ANSWER WAS IN THE COVERING SENTENCE, UNREAD. The Background File also holds nothing further about the donation or about any other deposit by Dr Griffiths, which answers a question the enquiry asked and which this archive likewise did not notice it had been given. THE RULE: READ THE COVERING LETTER, NOT ONLY THE ENCLOSURE. An archivist who goes to the trouble of answering in prose is a source, and the prose is part of the reply.
The list of what MSB 751 contains — published as “WHAT IT DOES CARRY”

IT WAS A SAMPLE PRESENTED AS AN INVENTORY. The letter was first read in a mail client’s PREVIEW OVERLAY on a screen eight hundred pixels wide, because this archive had declined to download the files. Nothing published from that reading was wrong. Opened properly as a PDF two days later, the same four pages also carry: DR PHILIP IN LONDON, “exceedingly glad” at the acceptance and promising to write to George himself — where this archive had him only as a courier; A JACKET AND WAISTCOAT FOR “JOHN” with “tell him his old father has sent it him, & to make haste to fill them out”; A YEAR OF NEWSPAPERS, one number lost by Henry “who has them every week, after I have done with them”; and FIVE NAMED FRIENDS OF THE HOUSE — Mr and Mrs Stanhope, Mr and Mrs Warner, Mrs Field and her daughters, and Miss Mary Field who had married a Mr Bellew, a surgeon. THE RULE: A DOCUMENT READ IN A PREVIEW IS NOT A DOCUMENT READ. If it is worth quoting it is worth opening.
The DSAB entry is wrong about exactly one thing, and its first source is a reference this archive did not have

BOTH HALVES WRONG, AND BY THE SAME CAUSE. The eleven-item source list was worked through WITHOUT FIRST BEING CHECKED AGAINST THIS ARCHIVE. Source 1, the death notice MOOC 6/9/35 no. 7698, HAS BEEN READ HERE SINCE BEFORE SEPTEMBER — it is published with two photographs and a transcription — and a work-list row was raised to order it. Struck. AND BECAUSE THE NOTICE WAS ALREADY IN HAND, THE ENTRY’S SECOND ERROR WAS THERE TO BE SEEN AND WAS NOT: Schoeman writes that the death notice records only eight children. IT NAMES TEN. So the archive published “wrong about exactly one thing” while holding the document that shows a second. The same reading also over-claimed Knapdaar as a new name to search; this archive already had it, from that same notice. THE RULE, WHICH IT ALREADY HAD AND DID NOT APPLY: a sweep that returns a name is checked against the archive before it is called a find — AND A BIBLIOGRAPHY IS A SWEEP.
